meta.titre: The Lymphatic System: from tissue fluid to lymph and back to the blood
meta.sous_theme: Tissue fluid, lymph vessels, lymph nodes and their functions

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: After a long bus journey from Douala to Bafoussam, a traveller notices that her ankles are slightly swollen, and the next week a child in the village has painful lumps under his jaw during a throat infection. Both events involve a second transport system that runs beside the blood system. The GCE asks about the fluid around cells, about lymph vessels and valves, and about the difference between lymph and blood plasma, so you need to understand how each fluid is formed and where it goes.

items: Blood plasma is the liquid part of blood; it carries dissolved food, waste and many proteins.
Capillaries are the tiniest blood vessels and have walls only one cell thick.
White blood cells defend the body against germs; phagocytes engulf them and lymphocytes make antibodies.

sections.titre: Tissue fluid, lymph, lymph vessels and lymph nodes
sections.contenu_markdown:
### From plasma to tissue fluid
Blood pressure forces some plasma out through the thin walls of the capillaries. This fluid is **tissue fluid**. It bathes every body cell and carries oxygen, glucose, amino acids and mineral salts to them, while waste such as carbon dioxide passes back. Large protein molecules and red blood cells are too big to leave the capillaries; some white blood cells (phagocytes) can squeeze through.

### From tissue fluid to lymph
Most tissue fluid returns to the blood capillaries. The rest enters the blind-ended **lymph capillaries**, and from then on it is called **lymph**. Lymph flows along lymph vessels, passes through **lymph nodes**, and is finally emptied into large veins near the neck, so it returns to the blood.

### Functions
1. Returns excess tissue fluid to the blood, so tissues do not swell.
2. Defends the body: lymph nodes contain lymphocytes and phagocytes, which trap and destroy germs.
3. Carries fats: the **lacteals** of the villi absorb fatty acids and glycerol into the lymph.

### Lymph and blood plasma

| Feature | Blood plasma | Lymph |
|---|---|---|
| Where found | Inside blood vessels | Inside lymph vessels and nodes |
| Proteins | Rich in plasma proteins | Fewer, because large proteins stay in the capillaries |
| Cells | None (it is the liquid part of blood) | Contains lymphocytes |
| Movement | Pushed by the heart | Moved slowly by muscle squeezing |
| Valves in the vessels | Only in veins (and in the heart) | Throughout the lymph vessels |

variantes.nom: How lymph moves and the role of valves
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why lymph flows one way although there is no pump
variantes.contenu_markdown: The lymphatic system has **no heart**. Lymph is moved when the skeletal muscles around the vessels contract and squeeze them as the body moves. The vessels contain **valves** like those in veins. The valves open to let lymph move towards the neck and close to prevent backflow, so the lymph moves in one direction only.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked about swollen glands or swollen limbs
variantes.contenu_markdown: During an infection the lymph nodes (for example in the neck, the armpit and the groin) become swollen and tender, because lymphocytes multiply there and phagocytes trap germs. If lymph vessels are blocked or damaged, tissue fluid collects and the tissue swells (**oedema**). In some tropical regions, tiny parasitic worms spread by mosquitoes can block lymph vessels and cause permanent swelling of a limb.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain how tissue fluid is formed in the body and how it eventually returns to the blood. *(6 marks)*

etapes.justification: "Explain how" needs a process with causes, in two parts: formation and return.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Part 1: formation of tissue fluid. Part 2: return of fluid by two routes.

etapes.justification: Name the cause (pressure) and the place (capillary walls).
etapes.resultat_markdown: Blood pressure forces plasma through the thin capillary walls.

etapes.justification: State which parts of the blood stay inside, to show the fluid is filtered.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Red blood cells and large proteins stay in the capillaries.

etapes.justification: Most of the fluid goes back into the blood capillaries.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Most tissue fluid re-enters the blood capillaries.

etapes.justification: The remainder takes the second route and becomes lymph.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The rest enters lymph capillaries, flows along lymph vessels and nodes, and empties into large veins near the neck.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Blood pressure forces plasma out through the thin walls of the capillaries to form tissue fluid, while red blood cells and large proteins stay inside. Most of this fluid goes back into the blood capillaries. The rest enters the lymph capillaries and becomes lymph, which flows through lymph vessels and lymph nodes and is emptied into large veins near the neck, so all the fluid returns to the blood.

items.erreur_markdown: Lymph is the same as blood because both are red.
items.pourquoi_faux: Lymph has no red blood cells. Plasma is also not red; it is the pale liquid in which the red cells are carried.
items.correction_markdown: Lymph is a clear fluid with no red blood cells, but with lymphocytes.

items.erreur_markdown: Tissue fluid and lymph are exactly the same fluid in the same place.
items.pourquoi_faux: Tissue fluid is outside the vessels, around cells. It is called lymph only after it has entered a lymph vessel.
items.correction_markdown: Tissue fluid bathes the cells; lymph is the fluid inside lymph vessels.

items.erreur_markdown: The heart pumps lymph around the body like blood.
items.pourquoi_faux: The heart is connected to the blood system only. Lymph is moved by muscles squeezing the vessels, and valves prevent backflow.
items.correction_markdown: Lymph flows slowly because it is squeezed by skeletal muscles and prevented from flowing back by valves.

items.pourquoi_faux: Plasma is made from the blood. Nodes are filters and defence centres that contain lymphocytes and phagocytes.
items.correction_markdown: Lymph nodes filter lymph and destroy germs.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Name the fluid that surrounds body cells. (b) State where the lymph enters the blood. (c) State two things done by lymph nodes.
items.solution_markdown: (a) **Tissue fluid**. (b) Into **large veins near the neck**. (c) Any two: they filter the lymph, trap germs, and contain lymphocytes that fight infection (and phagocytes that engulf germs).

items.enonce_markdown: In a simple model of one region of tissue, 36 cm$^3$ of fluid leaves the capillaries in one hour and 30 cm$^3$ returns to the capillaries. The rest drains into lymph vessels. (a) Calculate the volume of lymph formed in one hour. (b) Express it as a percentage of the fluid that left the capillaries (1 decimal place). (c) If the lymph vessels of this region became completely blocked, what volume of fluid would collect in 6 hours, and what would the person notice?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $36 - 30 =$ **6 cm$^3$**.

(b) $\frac{6}{36} \times 100 =$ **16.7%**.

(c) $6 \times 6 =$ **36 cm$^3$** would collect in the tissue, which would appear as swelling (oedema).

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Explain why the lymph nodes under a child's jaw swell and become painful during a throat infection. (b) Explain why a limb can swell when parasitic worms block its lymph vessels. (c) Explain why the fatty acids absorbed in the small intestine enter lymph vessels and not the blood capillaries of the villus.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Germs from the throat are carried in the lymph to the nearby nodes. Lymphocytes multiply there and phagocytes trap germs, so the nodes enlarge and become tender.

(b) The excess tissue fluid cannot drain away into the lymph vessels, so it collects in the tissue and the limb swells.

(c) After absorption, the fatty acids and glycerol are rebuilt into fats and pass into the **lacteal**, a lymph vessel in each villus. The lymph then carries them to large veins near the neck, so they join the blood.

items_markdown: Tissue fluid is formed when blood pressure forces plasma out of the capillaries; it bathes the cells and exchanges food and waste with them.
Excess tissue fluid enters lymph capillaries and becomes lymph, which is returned to the blood through large veins near the neck.
Lymph is moved by muscle squeezing, and valves in the lymph vessels allow flow in one direction only.
Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain lymphocytes and phagocytes; they swell during infection.
Compared with plasma, lymph has fewer proteins and contains lymphocytes; lacteals carry absorbed fats.
